{
  "need": "Belonging",
  "secondary": { "name": "Status", "description": "Sitting apart is also a way to protect dignity — if you never try, no one can visibly reject you." },
  "read": "A mid-year arrival missed all the early bonding that happens in September. The student likely feels like an outsider looking in at a group that already has its own shorthand, jokes, and seating arrangements. Protecting themselves from rejection by staying separate is a rational move, even if it deepens the isolation over time.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "Give the student space, assume they need time, and wait for them to come around on their own — which quietly allows the isolation to calcify and signals that no one is really watching out for them." },
  "mentorMove": "Create a low-stakes, face-saving on-ramp into the room's social life — not a forced introduction that spotlights the student, but a small role or pairing that makes connection happen naturally without requiring the student to take a vulnerable public leap.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "The expectation is that every student is a full member of this class community, not a visitor on the edges.",
    "You will keep engineering moments of genuine connection — not optional extras, but part of how this room works."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "The student gets to choose which partner activity, which small group, or which seat shift feels least threatening.",
    "The first bridge can be built around a task or shared interest rather than overt socializing — let the relationship grow as a side effect of doing something together."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I've been meaning to catch you for a second. Jumping into a class mid-year is genuinely one of the harder things — everyone else already has their thing going and you're figuring out where you fit. That's a real adjustment." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "Can I ask — is there anything about how the class runs that feels like it's working for you so far, or anything that's felt a bit awkward to navigate?" },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "I'm going to pair people up for the next project and I want to be deliberate about it. You don't have to tell me who you'd pick, but are there people you've noticed you might want to work with, or a type of task where you feel more in your element? I'll use that." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I want you to know I hold everyone in here to the same standard — full participation, real contribution — and I'm not making an exception for you because I think you can absolutely do that. I'm just going to make sure the setup actually gives you a fair shot at it." }
  ],
  "longGame": "Check back briefly after the first paired activity — not to evaluate the social outcome, but to ask how the work went. Over a few weeks, the goal is that this student has at least one peer who knows their name and what they're good at, which shifts them from guest to member."
}
situation: A student who joined mid-year sits apart and has not connected with anyone.
